title: Paul speaks in a substituted persona, not as himself
english: By doing good works the divine apostle became an unspotted image for his disciples. That is why he also cried out: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1). So what he said is not literally about himself: “I know that good does not dwell in my flesh” (Romans 7:18), nor “Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:24). Rather, he says these things and all such things in a substituted persona, speaking in character to refute those who love sin.

Just as divine Scripture knows how to call human beings fleshly, soulish, spiritual, and by countless other names based on their own actions, so too it knows how to call the devil not only Satan, the Adversary, the devil, the Serpent, the Lion, and Beliar, but also flesh and law and sin and death. For we were enslaved to these through disobedience, and not to Christ. That is why he says: “When we were in the flesh” (Romans 7:5), making clear that they are no longer in the flesh, even though they are in the flesh. So he is not slandering the flesh we wear, but the flesh called by the same name, from which we have also been set free because we died in Christ by being buried together with him through baptism. We have truly been freed from this flesh. For he adds: “But now we have been released from the law of sin, having died to that which held us captive, so that we serve in newness of the Spirit and not in oldness of the letter” (Romans 7:6).

Then he began again the hypothetical speaking in character, starting from “What then shall we say? Is the law sin? By no means!” (Romans 7:7) up to “Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:24). He laid down an unshaken foundation in his prologue, defending himself by saying: “What then? Is the law sin? By no means!” (Romans 7:7), and that “the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good” (Romans 7:12). Here he means by “law” not the one warring against the law of our mind, but the one that warns beforehand, the one that punishes those who sin. That is why he also agreed with it as holy and just and good.

Then he began again to explain in sequence what he had said earlier, prefacing it with a word of thanksgiving: “I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:25). Then, to condemn those who take occasion from such things and revile the flesh we wear, he asks in the form of a question: “So then, do I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin?” Is Paul himself divided, serving the law of God in one part and the law of sin in another? Do I have Christ and Beliar in myself at the same time and in the same place? Do I, who say “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20), have sin living in me, having lied? I who proclaimed to others: “Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit within you?” (1 Corinthians 6:19), and “Glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:20), do I myself have nothing good in my body? But Paul is not such a person; he is not. By no means! For though he was formerly a child of wrath and a vessel of wrath, having changed his manner, not his nature, he became a precious vessel of election.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
orientation: Didymus opens his commentary on Romans 7 by arguing that Paul's words about the wretched man and indwelling sin are spoken in a borrowed character, not about Paul himself or any Christian buried with Christ in baptism.
